observation_summary: The StopWatch.stop() method incorrectly updates the stopTime even when the stopwatch is already suspended, causing the total time to increase erroneously after a stop() call.
hypothesis: The stop() method lacks a conditional check to ensure that stopTime is only updated if the stopwatch is currently in the RUNNING state. If it is already SUSPENDED, the stopTime should not be recalculated.
prediction: The fix will involve wrapping the stopTime assignment in an 'if' statement that checks if the current state is STATE_RUNNING.
experiment_rationale: The provided fix diff shows exactly this: an 'if(this.runningState == STATE_RUNNING)' guard was added around the 'stopTime = System.currentTimeMillis();' assignment, confirming the hypothesis.
reasoning_summary: The bug is caused by a missing validation check (guard) in the stop() method. The method was unconditionally updating the stop time, even when the stopwatch was already suspended. Adding the missing state check ensures the stop time is only captured when the stopwatch is actively running, which is the correct behavior for a stopwatch component.
evidence_used: The bug report states: 'suspend() acts as split(), if followed by stop()'
The fix diff shows: 'if(this.runningState == STATE_RUNNING) { stopTime = System.currentTimeMillis(); }'

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the logic is procedural, the root cause is specifically the absence of a guard condition to prevent an incorrect state transition/value update, which is the definition of a Checking defect.
